title: Low blood sugar in someone with diabetes (hypoglycaemia)
summary: Someone with diabetes who is sweating, shaky, pale, confused, or aggressive may have low blood sugar. Sugar by mouth — if they can swallow — works fast.
steps: Help them sit or lie down somewhere safe.
If they are alert and can swallow, give a fast-acting sugar: 4–5 glucose tablets, half a cup of fruit juice or regular fizzy drink, 3 teaspoons of sugar in water, or a tablespoon of honey/jam.
Wait 10–15 minutes. If they have not improved, give the same dose of fast sugar again.
Once they feel better, give a slower carbohydrate snack to keep sugar steady: a piece of bread, a biscuit, a banana, or a meal if it is due.
Help them check their blood sugar if they have a meter, and note what happened (last insulin dose, last meal, recent activity).
Stay with them for at least an hour. Even after they recover, they should not drive for several hours.
avoid: Do not give insulin — that is the doctor's job. The aim of first aid is to raise blood sugar, not lower it further.
Do not give anything by mouth if they are too drowsy to swallow safely, unresponsive, or having a seizure — call emergency instead.
Do not assume they are drunk or angry on purpose — low sugar mimics both.
Do not skip the slow carbohydrate snack — sugar alone wears off quickly.
whenToEscalate: Emergency immediately if: they are unconscious or cannot swallow, having a seizure, drowsy and unable to drink, or do not improve after two fast-sugar doses 15 minutes apart.
Anyone who has had a hypo while alone, while driving, or near machinery — see their diabetes team for review.
Repeated hypos over days or weeks — needs urgent diabetes review.
First-ever hypo in someone newly diagnosed — see the diabetes team that day.
specialty: Emergency department for severe hypos; diabetes team / general physician for follow-up.
